endorsements.quote: Establish regular monitoring of error rates, mindful of the need for continual review processes given the ever-changing nature of GenAI algorithms.

Equally, we should also seek to empower individuals to make their own decisions about using GenAI to support their health needs, and engage end-users throughout the design, implementation, evaluation, and governance processes, recognizing that existing tools, without tailoring for a healthcare context, are already in widespread use globally.
Partnership with community organizations is crucial to ensuring the needs and concerns of target end-users are heard and integrated throughout the design and implementation process.

We emphasize the importance of transparent reporting, including details of how AI systems were designed and trained, alongside disclosures of conflicts of interest and publication of negativefindings in afield where commercial and public priorities are often tightly intertwined.
The intended health impact of an intervention and corresponding outcome metrics should be clearly defined from the design phase.
Consider whether GenAI is the highest impact way of addressing your use case, taking into account existing basic healthcare and digital infrastructure.

unlisted_practices: Only use GenAI tools when impact and cost-effectiveness modelling indicate they are likely to provide advantages over existing methods.
Consider acceptable error rates for specific use cases, including the impact of errors and existing human error rates.
Use prompt engineering or retrieval augmented generation to provide more domain-specific responses and reduce errors.
Maintain rigorous human-in-the-loop oversight of implemented GenAI tools where errors would detriment patient care.
Review the data safeguards and policies of any potential LLM provider, considering the type of data analyzed and the suitability of the model employed.
Ensure you have the rights to use training data.
Integrate automated scanning to detect and flag sensitive data before it reaches models.
Consider trade-offs between data utility and data protection and employ specific privacy-enhancing technologies where appropriate.
Invest in the development of diverse language datasets and language-specific benchmarks for model quality and accuracy.
Test and train LLM-enabled tools on data relevant to the intended healthcare setting.
Prioritize investment in basic healthcare infrastructure alongside digital interventions.
Assess organizational digital readiness before implementing any AI tools.
Develop algorithms that include checks against bias and discrimination.
Establish legal governance frameworks to ensure adherence to best practices in Responsible AI.
Use the STANDING Together recommendations to support transparency regarding limitations of health datasets and proactive evaluation of their effect across population groups.
Understand and monitor how adversarial actors are using GenAI and establish appropriate mitigations.
Establish forums for organizations to share interim results, benchmarks, and learnings from GenAI pilots.
Use the CONSORT-AI extension for reporting clinical trials of AI interventions.
Conduct continuous evaluation and review of GenAI tools because outputs constantly evolve.
Evaluate GenAI tools on correctness, completeness, time and cost savings, understandability, empathy, and appropriateness of tone.
Consider opportunity costs of not testing GenAI tools when weighing safety and potential benefits.
Foster experimentation in lower-risk GenAI applications while applying appropriate controls in higher-risk settings.
Use shared infrastructure for models trained on local languages to reduce costs of non-Western languages.
Reduce the energy footprint of AI through efficient training algorithms, smaller architectures, and optimized hardware.

screen.reason: This is a perspective article presenting a framework for evaluating and governing generative AI in healthcare based on roundtable discussions and expert interviews.
